Take a walk into an ancient forest
after an autumn rain.
As you step across damp pine
needles, the rich smell of soil
fills the air.
Near the base of an old trunk,
you spot a small mushroom quietly
pushing its way through the moss.
It looks delicate, soft,
and easy to overlook.
We think of mushrooms and molds
as background players, tiny
recyclers cleaning up fallen leaves
beneath towering oaks and pines.
But have you ever wondered what
the world looked like before trees
even existed?
Imagine stepping out of a time
machine onto dry land over four
hundred million years ago.
The first thing you notice is the silence.
There are no birds in the branches
above you, no rustling leaves,
and no flowers along the hills.
In fact, there is nothing overhead at all.
The sky stretches uninterrupted
across barren valleys and rocky plains.
If you look down at your boots,
the plant life barely reaches your ankles.
The earliest land plants are
creeping stems without leaves,
clinging to damp mud.
In a world where every living thing
is miniature, how tall could
anything possibly grow?
You turn toward the horizon,
and your eyes catch something impossible.
Rising from the flat,
rock-strewn plain are massive,
stone-colored pillars, standing
straight against the wind.
They look like chimneys or telephone
poles, casting long shadows across
the low green carpet of moss.
Some of these spires reach eight
meters into the sky,
nearly twenty-six feet above the bare ground.
Their bases are up to a meter thick.
If you reached out to touch one,
you would feel no rough bark and
no sticky sap.
So what was this silent giant?
This prehistoric mystery is known
to science as Prototaxites.
In the nineteenth century,
a Canadian geologist named John
William Dawson described its
petrified trunks, and he thought
they were the wood of ancient conifers.
The fossils did look like weathered
logs, and the name Prototaxites
means first yew.
After all, what else could grow
into a trunk eight meters tall?
But as microscopes improved,
a strange problem appeared.
Where were the growth rings,
and where were the plant cells?
When researchers sliced through
the fossils, they found no wood
fibers and no plant cell walls.
Instead, they found a dense,
tightly woven mass of microscopic
tubes, some hollow and some filled
with thinner filaments.
This structure looked nothing like a tree.
It looked far more like the body
of a fungus.
Could the tallest organism on land,
at the dawn of life on land,
have been a gigantic fungus?
To see why that is so strange,
think about what a mushroom really is.
The mushroom you spotted in the
moss is only the visible part,
a fruiting body that exists to release spores.
The real organism is hidden
underground, a web of fine threads
called hyphae, which together make
up the mycelium.
These threads dissolve and absorb
their food from the outside.
Most fungi never grow large above
ground, because soft threads and
soft caps cannot hold up much weight.
Fungi can still reach huge sizes, though.
In the Malheur National Forest
in Oregon, a honey fungus called
Armillaria ostoyae spreads through
the soil across almost ten square
kilometers, according to the United
States Forest Service.
It is one of the largest living
things on Earth, and almost all
of it is hidden below your feet.
Prototaxites would have been the opposite.
A giant fungus on this scale would
have stood in plain sight,
tall and thick, with nothing hiding it.
The idea sounded absurd.
Fungi are supposed to be soft,
short-lived, and hidden in dark
corners, not standing like stone
monuments against the wind.
In 2001, the paleobotanist Francis
Hueber argued that these fossils
were the remains of a giant fungus,
and the debate caught fire.
For years, scientists argued.
Some suggested a giant seaweed
that had washed ashore.
Others proposed a lichen,
a partnership between a fungus
and an alga.
Still others pictured a huge
rolled-up mat of liverworts.
But however researchers examined
the tubes, many kept pointing back
to the fungal kingdom.
Then came a clue from chemistry.
In 2007, geochemists measured the
carbon isotopes preserved in
Prototaxites fossils.
Plants draw carbon straight from
the air, so their isotope signatures
stay fairly consistent.
But the signatures in Prototaxites
varied widely between specimens.
That fits an organism that was
not making food from sunlight,
but absorbing nourishment from
whatever decaying matter surrounded it.
Scientists call such an organism
a heterotroph.
That picture changed how we see
this lost world.
Prototaxites was probably not a
tree sunbathing in the Silurian light.
It was more likely an immense
decomposer, feeding on organic
crusts, mats of early plants,
and the remains of tiny microbes.
While modern molds spread invisible
threads through damp bread or a
basement wall, this ancient giant
built a tower.
For roughly forty million years,
from the Silurian into the Devonian,
the tallest things on dry land
were not plants or animals.
They were very likely fungi.
To put that in perspective,
modern humans have existed for
only a few hundred thousand years.
The giants stood for more than
one hundred times longer than we have.
Now a word of honesty,
because science is never finished.
In 2025, a research team reported
a preprint, not yet peer reviewed,
that found no trace of chitin,
the material that normally builds
fungal cell walls.
They suggest that Prototaxites
might belong to an entire branch
of life that has no living relatives.
So the exact family tree of these
giants is still an open question.
Either way, what stood on that
plain was something truly extraordinary.
Picture that landscape at dusk.
There is no grass,
because grass would not evolve
for hundreds of millions of years.
There are no flowers,
no insects buzzing, and no dinosaurs.
Dinosaurs would not appear for
well over one hundred million years.
The only tall things in sight are
these pale towers, each one standing
alone, and each one older than
anything a human has ever seen.
Have you ever wondered what life
was like at the foot of such a giant?
Crawling around its base were some
of the first land animals:
tiny armored millipedes, primitive
springtails, and early relatives
of spiders and scorpions.
To creatures this small,
a single trunk was less a landmark
than a mountain, and perhaps a
source of shade, shelter, and moisture.
Researchers have even described
tunnels and chambers inside fossil
Prototaxites.
Some of those were probably dug
by early arthropods, much like
beetles burrowing into rotting wood today.
In a world with no forests to
cast deep shade, these towers may
have offered shelter from harsh
wind and strong ultraviolet light.
They may have been a hub for
fragile communities of tiny animals
on an otherwise empty planet.
But we should be careful here.
Fossil burrows show that animals
used the trunks.
They cannot tell us exactly how
important the giants were to the ecosystem.
Still, a bigger question lingers.
Why would any living thing invest
so much energy in a spire as
tall as a two-story building?
One hypothesis is about reproduction.
Fungi release microscopic spores
into the air and rely on breezes
to carry their offspring.
Near the ground, friction slows
the wind to a crawl.
By lifting its spore-making tissue
eight meters up, a giant could
launch millions of spores into
faster air, sending its genes
drifting across a continent.
Another hypothesis treats the tower
as a storage tank.
In an early land environment with
unpredictable rains and drying
winds, holding on to water was
a matter of life and death.
A thick column of tissue could
store water and nutrients gathered
in wet periods, and carry the
organism through a drought while
the low mosses around it withered.
Nobody knows for sure which idea
is right, and both could be partly true.
Whatever the reason, the design
worked for a very long time.
But the reign of the giants could
not last forever.
Beneath their shadow, a quiet
revolution was beginning.
Green plants were no longer content
to creep along the mud.
Over millions of years they
developed rigid plumbing that could
lift water upward, tough compounds
that stiffened their stems,
and broad leaves that captured sunlight.
The first true trees,
like Archaeopteris, appeared in
the Devonian, around three hundred
and eighty-five million years ago.
Their deep roots helped turn bare
rock into soil, and they spread
across the continents in dense forests.
Archaeopteris could grow to about
thirty meters tall, nearly four
times the height of the tallest Prototaxites.
For the first time,
the skyline belonged to green wood and leaves.
The fungal towers, once alone on
the horizon, were now standing
in the shade of something taller.
Imagine looking up from the base
of an eight-meter pillar and seeing
a leafy crown high above you.
It must have been a very different
world from the one the giants had
known for tens of millions of years.
How could a fungal spire survive
in a world of leafy crowns?
Scientists suspect it could not.
Forest canopies cast deep shade
over the surface crusts and mats
that the giants may have fed on.
The new wood of the first trees
was also tough, and fungi of the
time may not yet have had the
tools to break it down easily.
Whatever the exact cause,
Prototaxites faded from the fossil
record by the Late Devonian.
The age of the fungal pillars was over.
Yet this was not a defeat for fungi.
Fungi did not vanish.
Fungi as a whole kept going,
and spread their thread-like
networks, called mycelium, through
the dark, fertile soil,
recycling the remains of the plants
that had taken the sky.
In fact, partnerships between fungi
and plant roots are far older than forests.
Fossils from around four hundred
million years ago already show
fungi living inside the tissues
of early land plants.
Scrape away the top layer of dirt
in any woodland today,
and you will meet the legacy of
that transition.
Beneath your feet lies a hidden
labyrinth of white threads wrapping
around the roots of trees.
This underground system is called
a mycorrhizal network.
Fungi deliver minerals, nitrogen,
and water from the soil to the roots.
In return, trees send down sugars
made in their sunlit leaves.
An ancient rivalry has become an
alliance, and most of the plants
on Earth depend on it.
Isn't it fascinating how history
can flip the roles of living things?
Over four hundred million years
ago, fragile plants cowered in
the shadow of giant spires.
Today, enormous trees reach for
the sun, while mushrooms pop up
humbly around their trunks.
Yet without the fungal world below,
breaking down dead wood and feeding
roots, forests would choke under
their own debris.
The next time you walk through
a quiet park, pause near a patch of moss.
Look up at the oak or spruce
above you, then look down at the
small, pale mushroom beside your shoe.
Beneath that quiet cap lies a
lineage that reaches back to a
forgotten chapter of our planet's history.
Long before leaves whispered in
the breeze, the world may have
belonged to silent, towering spires,
standing proud beneath a lonely sky.
Perhaps the giants never truly vanished.
Perhaps they simply learned to
rule from beneath the earth.
